learningObjective: Compare warp-shuffle intra-warp reductions with shared-memory tree reductions for a per-block sum.

canonicalClaims.claim: The canonical CUDA block-reduce uses __shfl_down_sync inside each warp, followed by one SMEM write per warp, one __syncthreads(), and one final warp-shuffle reduce over the warp-level partials. This is faster than a pure SMEM tree and much faster than block-wide atomicAdd for dense reductions.
conditions: Block size is a multiple of warpSize.
Reduction is over a value type supported by __shfl_down_sync (int/float/double via reinterpretation).
nonImplications: Does not imply shuffles beat SMEM in every scenario.
Does not imply atomicAdd is always bad.

misconceptions.claim: Shared-memory tree reductions are the fastest option on modern GPUs.
misconceptions.whyWrong: SMEM tree needs multiple __syncthreads() and has higher latency than shuffle-based reductions.

misconceptions.claim: Block-wide atomicAdd is the fastest way to reduce.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Contention on the atomic target serializes writes and is much slower for dense reductions.

misconceptions.claim: All reduction strategies produce bit-identical FP32 results.
misconceptions.whyWrong: FP addition is non-associative; different summation orders produce different roundings.

implementationFacts: __shfl_down_sync has a 32-lane butterfly pattern reaching a warp-level scalar in 5 rounds.
Modern kernels also use __reduce_add_sync (sm_80+) or cooperative_groups reduce for the same effect.
performanceScenarios: Softmax, LayerNorm, RMSNorm, and dot products all rely on this pattern for per-row reduction.
